prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this moire platform

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is, in my judgement, the cleanest recent case of a quantitative prediction followed by a decisive experimental discovery in correlated-electron physics. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model located the magic angle and the flat bands from a simple, controlled starting point; the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity then showed that a single tunable device could host strong-correlation physics that previously required chemistry and high pressure. The consequences are broad: a whole family of moire materials, tunable Chern bands and fractional Chern insulators, and a new meeting point for ab initio band-structure methods and many-body theory, which is exactly where my own field is being pushed. It has been reproduced by many independent groups over roughly eight years, and the flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology is firmly established even though the pairing mechanism is not. I weight the discovery of a new, general platform more heavily than settling every mechanism question.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The superconducting pairing mechanism is unresolved, twist-angle disorder and sample dependence complicate what is intrinsic, and the credited list omits Yuan Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, as well as earlier twisted-bilayer band theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and other moire experimentalists. Compared with optical lattice clocks, which are mature, independently confirmed at the 1e-18 level and cleanly attributed to two people, this candidate is less settled and its credit is messier. The 2016 prize on topological phases also means the committee may prefer a more distinct condensed-matter subject.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B005 third and calls it somewhat early but defensible, because the superconducting pairing is still debated and the interpretation is not fully stable; he ranks the lattice clocks first.
responses.response: I accept that the pairing mechanism is open, but I would not make it the test of maturity. The criterion is the discovery and its robustness, and here the flat-band prediction, the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes have all been reproduced by many groups and probed with transport, tunnelling and scanning-probe spectroscopy. High-temperature superconductivity was recognised in 1987 without an agreed mechanism. Where I do agree with Kroll is that the lattice clock case is the safer one on every maturity metric, and I would not be troubled if the committee preferred B007; I simply think the novelty and breadth of the moire platform are larger.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first as an original, clean idea with broad measurable impact across metrology, relativistic geodesy and searches for new physics, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second while calling the timing arguably early.
responses.response: I share her view of the clocks as a genuine invention with exceptional measurable impact, and my second-place ranking reflects that. Where I disagree is on 'arguably early': eight years of replication, extension to other moire systems and a very large theory-experiment literature make this timely rather than premature. I also press the metrology overlap she herself flags. Frequency combs (2005) and single-ion control (2012) already honoured neighbouring precision-AMO work, so the committee must justify another prize in that corridor, whereas moire quantum matter has no prize of its own. That is a reason to rank B005 slightly ahead, not a reason to dismiss B007.

responses.point: Mehlig proposes only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero for B005, a two-person theory plus experiment pairing, and notes that Bistritzer's contribution is decisive for the theory while an experimental co-discoverer would also be argued; he ranks hexatic melting (B025) first.
responses.response: Bistritzer co-authored the 2011 prediction as first author and did the explicit magic-angle computation with MacDonald, so I disagree with dropping him: the prediction is the defining theoretical result and a fair prize should credit its authors. I would rather keep three names than force an arbitrary two. I also respectfully disagree with ranking B025 above B005: the two-step melting picture is elegant and mature, but it sits close to the 2016 recognition of defect-mediated topological phases and has far less contemporary traction than moire matter. I would accept it as a late-recognition alternative, but not as the lead.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, stresses that interface and stacking control are judged by materials standards, and flags sample-to-sample twist-angle inhomogeneity as complicating what is intrinsic.
responses.response: I agree on the discovery and appreciate the materials point; twist-angle disorder is real and is partly why the pairing question is hard. It does not undermine the core phenomenology, which scanning-probe and transport studies on cleaner devices have supported. We differ on credit: she leaves out Bistritzer to keep a focused citation, whereas I think the three-name theory-plus-experiment configuration is the more accurate description of what was discovered. She is right that Cao's omission is a genuine injustice that the supplied credit list cannot repair. Her third-place topological insulator grouping with Hasan but without Mele also seems to me a harder attribution than mine.

responses.point: Pearce ranks optical lattice clocks first as an instrument breakthrough with repeated, quantitative payoff, ranks magic-angle graphene second while worrying that the omission of the first experimental author makes the attribution imperfect, and ranks IceCube third.
responses.response: I agree that clocks are a clear instrument breakthrough and that the attribution of B007 is simpler. On the Cao issue I take the concern seriously, but the limit of three people is a structural constraint that affects any collaborative discovery; here the originating theorists and the leader of the experimental programme are clearly identifiable. I would be wary of letting the clean two-name attribution of B007 decide the outcome by itself, since that would systematically favour instrument and metrology prizes over collaborative condensed-matter discoveries.

uncertainties: Whether a prize on moire matter is judged premature because the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled.
How to handle the omission of Yuan Cao (first author of the 2018 experiments) and earlier twisted-bilayer band theory, and whether Jarillo-Herrero alone is the right experimental credit.
Whether the committee prefers the better-settled lattice-clock prize (B007) given the overlap concerns about earlier metrology prizes in 2005 and 2012.
Whether moire families beyond twisted graphene (twisted WSe2, fractional Chern insulators) belong in the same citation or should wait.
I rely on recalled priority history rather than verified records, particularly for the 2011 and 2018 papers.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the preferred B005 trio. My field proximity is the relevant disclosure: I work on first-principles and many-body electronic-structure theory and two-dimensional materials, which could bias me toward moire quantum matter and toward theory-plus-experiment prizes in correlated electrons, and I should be challenged on that. The profile documents no connection to MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori or Ye.
